ai.summary: A new study tested the software used to predict how much power offshore wind farms will produce, comparing its estimates with real turbine records from six North Sea-area farms over about 4.5 years. Overall the models landed within about 5% of actual output, but they differed in how well they handled wake losses, the energy lost when one farm's turbines slow the wind for others. The best-performing version was found to work well when turbines are spaced into separate grid cells, though it is not a replacement for detailed layout design tools.
points: Study covered July 2017 to December 2021 over the German Bight, using minute-by-minute turbine output data from six offshore farms
Total energy yield estimates were within ±5% of real figures, and the base weather model slightly underestimated wind speed
The Fitch-pAIM variant performed best at fine grid resolution, but the models are suited to annual yield estimates rather than turbine layout decisions
ai.why: For business owners in offshore energy supply or related projects, more reliable yield forecasts may affect how project costs and returns are estimated, though the study does not change any financial outlook directly.
